Inflammations Of The Musculoskeletal System

Carolina Solomon, Man

14.1. Osteomyelitis

It is defifined as the septic infection or inflflammation of the connective tissue of the bone. This disease has a higher incidence in the fifirst decade (2-12 years of age), male gender being more frequently affected (M: F = 3:1). Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequently involved pathogenic agent. It is spreading through the blood flflow, direct inoculation, contiguity or iatrogenic pathways (after surgery).

Radio­imaging aspects:

1. Early stage

Bone changes: at 10-21 days after the onset, osteoporosis appears, followed by osteolysis located in the medullary canal, with diffuse appearance, associated with periosteal reaction (3-6 weeks after the onset). Soft tissue changes: edema after 7-14 days of infection.

X-ray: lower utility at this stage; radiological signs are usually detected after 2-3 weeks from the onset.

US: helpful technique for the identifification of edema and cellulitis surrounding the infection site.

MRI: detects the juxtaphyseal medullary edema (hypersignal on T2 sequence, hyposignal on T1 sequence), with contrast enhancement at the pathological changes level. nuela Lenghel, Sorin M. Dudea

2. Acute stage

X-ray: identififies the necrotic bony fragment (sequestrum) surrounded by an osteolytic area (cloaca), delineated by a sclerotic opaque rim (involucrum); periosteal reaction and endosteal osteosclerosis are associated; the latter may lead to the disappearance of the medullary canal (fifigure 95).

CT: characterizes outstandingly the changes detected at X­ray examination.

MRI is usually very useful in spine osteomyelitis, with very high resolution for the small parts changes.

3. Healing stage

It is characterized by changing the standard bone structure, with fifibrosis, irregular osteosclerosis and hyperostosis of the bone. The complications that may appear are represented by arthritis, pathological bone fracture and deformities of the limbs.

4. Clinical and peculiar imaging aspects:

Bone whitlow. Whitlow is an infection that appears at the level of the soft tissues of the fifingers. Bone whitlow designates the progression of the infection to the bone. The infection initially destroys the periosteum and afterward produces focal osteolysis or may involve the entire phalanx; no periosteal reaction is, therefore, present (fifigure 96).

14.2. Arthritis

14.2.1. Septic arthritis

Path of infection. Inoculation of the synovial membrane may be direct or indirect. In the case of direct inoculation, the pathogen can reach the joint by spreading from an infection confifined to the soft tissues, secondary to a penetrating lesion or post arthroplasty, and a neighboring outbreak of osteomyelitis. Indirect inoculation of the synovial membrane is performed hematogenous. The most common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus, gonococcus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Candida albicans.

Clinical presentation. The diagnosis of septic arthritis is established in a clinical context, the changes being nonspecifific, respectively the presence of Celsian signs at the level of the affected joint. The damage is monoarticular in most cases, and in half of the cases, the blood cultures are positive. In the case of gonococcal arthritis, dermatitis can be found in 66% of the cases. There are several age groups considered at risk: children < 3 years (in whom the singled out joint is septic hip); teenagers; the elderly (due to chronic diseases and arthroplasties). There are also categories of population or clinical situations at risk: patients with chronic diseases ± corticosteroid therapy, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, end­stage renal disease, i.v. drug use, HIV / AIDS disease and post­joint surgery ± prostheses.

Relevant pathology. The morphopathophysiological sequence is initiated by the synovial infection, which leads to edema and hypertrophy; subsequently, the appearance of exudative intraarticular flfluid occurs, followed by cartilaginous destruction, determined by the action of proteolytic enzymes. In some cases, the presence of pathological changes in the underlying bone can be observed, determining the appearance of erosions and osteomyelitis.

Imaging aspects. Although any joint can present the disease, there is a particular predilection for some joints in specifific situations. Thus, in children, the hip joints are affected more frequently; in adults, the knee joint, respectively the sacroiliac or sternoclavicular ones in diabetics, HIV / AIDS or i.v. drug use.

At fifirst, the X-ray appearance may be normal. As the disease progresses, non­

Fig. 97. Septic arthritis. Note the irre- gularity of the bone surfaces in the tibiotarsal joint (arrows).

14. IINFLAMMATIO specifific signs appear, the fifirst being the intra-articular flfluid. In the next phase, hyperemia causes the appearance of periarticular osteoporosis. Subsequently, cartilaginous destruction occurs, which causes the joint space to narrow. Other observed signs are blurred appearance of the bone cortex, destruction of the subchondral bone and marginal erosions, osteomyelitis. Sclerotic reaction occurs in bacterial infection. Ankylosis is rare (fifigure 97).

CT is rarely used. The changes highlighted on CT are similar to those found in the X­ray investigation. CT can detect erosion and sclerosis in regions more diffificult to assess by X-ray (sacroiliac, respectively sternoclavicular joints). Aspiration of intra­articular collections for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes can be performed under CT guidance.

MRI has very high sensitivity and specifificity in diagnosing septic arthritis compared to other imaging methods. Joint changes are detectable on MRI 24 hours after the onset of the disease. There is a subchondral hyposignal on both sides of the joint in the T1-weighted sequence. Intra-

Postcontrast enhancement is found in the thickened synovial, at the level of the subchondral bone and, in some cases, in abscesses in the adjacent soft tissues.

Intra­articular collections in small quantities are detected with great accuracy by ultrasound. US is the method of choice for assessing the collections in the hip joint in children and guiding aspiration. In the acute phase of the disease, Doppler reveals a vascular signal in the thickened synovia. Articular punctures can be performed under ultrasound guidance, both for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, by intra­articular administration of anti-inflflammatory drugs and antibiotics (fifigure 98).

Examination algorithm. The fifirst imaging method of examining septic arthritis remains X­ray, which detects intra­articular collection, bone and cartilage destruction. This technique has low sensitivity in the early stages and is nonspecifific in later stages. Important: The radio­imaging characteristics of septic arthritis are:

­ in the acute phase: intra­articular collection, periarticular osteoporosis, swelling of the periarticular soft tissues;

­ late phase: destruction of cartilage and subchondral bone, on both sides of the joint, with the possibility of bone ankylosis.

14.2.2. Non-infectious arthritis

14.2.2.1. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, systemic inflflammatory disease with primary damage to the joints. It most commonly affects the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), intercarpal, PIP (proximal interphalangeal), MTP (metatarsophalangeal), shoulder, elbow and knee joints. The general population incidence is ≈ 1%, female being affected more frequently (F: M = 3: 1), in the interval 30-50 years. The disease evolves differently in each patient, having a variable appearance, with outbreaks and remissions.

Clinic. RA is a symmetrical polyarthritis that affects the hands and feet’s small joints, accompanied by states of fatigue, morning joint stiffness, joint pain, fever; it is long­standing.

Relevant pathology. Synovial thickening/hypertrophy, joint distension, bone erosions, cartilaginous destruction and destruction of the subchondral bone are observed in this order. The cause of RA’s changes is the accumulation of CD4 T helper cells; increased production of immunoglobulins, including rheumatoid factor. The trigger for changes in the joint is represented by synovial angiogenesis.

Imaging aspects. Being a pure erosive disease, RA causes erosions; cartilage narrowing; altering bones’ alignment in the joints and joint deformities; osteoporosis and fifinally, bone ankylosis.

RX: RA is classically located in the small joints of the hands, causing symmetrical changes, even if, in the early stages, the damage can be unilateral.

­ In the early phase, the condition is located at the level of the MCP, radio­carpal (RC), radio­ulnar (RU) joints. In the late stage, the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and intercarpal joints are affected. Distal interphalangeal joints (DIP) are seldom affected.

­ In the beginning, the soft tissues’ focal swelling is observed, the fifirst affected being the MCP and PIP joints and ulnar styloid (fifigure 99).

  • - Osteoporosis is another sign highlighted< in RA. Early on, osteoporosis is localized juxta­articular, with a striped appearance; late being diffusely highlighted ­ In the early stages, erosions appear as< reduced cortical differentiation, going as far as the “dot­dash” appearance. Marginal erosions appear as “mouse ears” at the phalanges’ base, ulnar or radial styloid. The localization of erosions at the level of the subchondral bone has the appearance of the “inkwell frame”. It can destroy the distal ulna and the proximal carpus (fifigure 100).

  • - The articular space has a varied aspect,< depending on the evolution phase of the disease.     US is an excellent imaging method for detecting small amounts of intra­articular or tendon flfluid. Thickening of the synovial membrane, characteristic of arthritis, especially RA, called the articular pannus, is very well highlighted using ultrasound. Doppler techniques allow the evaluation of the synovial pannus’ hypervascularization, contributing to the establishment of activity outbreaks, which is very important for establishing the optimal therapeutic scheme. Rheumatoid nodules appear on ultrasound in the form of hypoechoic homogeneous nodular lesions.

    In RA, MRI helps detect: joint pannus, flfluid collection, bone edema, erosions, subchondral cysts and tendon changes. Post­contrast enhancement is observed in the articular pannus, as well as with intraand peritendinous location.

    Examination algorithm. The fifirst examination performed is the X­ray. If this is negative, the evaluation is continued with US or MRI to diagnose the disease’s early stages. Dynamic, post­therapeutic followup is performed using ultrasound, including Doppler techniques, for visualizing the synovitis and intra­articular collection, respectively, using MRI to detect erosions.

    THM: RA is more common in middle­aged women, the most affected joints being the small ones of the hands. US and MRI are used for early diagnosis, while the essential radiological examination remains comparative hand X­ray.

    14.2.2.2. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS)

    AS is a progressive chronic inflflammatory arthropathy and enthesopathy that mainly affects the axial skeleton (synovial ONS OF THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM l 123 joints and soft tissues adjacent to the spine and sacroiliac – SI- joints). However, other joints, such as the hip, shoulder or knee, may be involved. The AS incidence is 0.1% in the population, with the age of onset between 15 and 30 years and more common in males (M: F = 2.5-5:1). AS has a multigenic inherited genetic component, primarily associated with HLA-B27.

    Clinic: AS presents an insidious onset, with low back pain and stiffness. Asymmetric oligoarticular peripheral disease may be encountered.Associated,thereisareduction in chest expansion <4 cm. Frequently these patients show extraarticular signs, such as pulmonary fifibrosis, heart disorders, aortic insuffificiency, spinal cord compression or amyloidosis. Also, the patients may present nonspecifific signs and symptoms: fever, loss of appetite, fatigue and weight loss.

    Relevant pathology. Diffuse proliferative synovitis of diarthrodial joints occurs in AS, with changes similar to those found in RA.

    X-Ray. The presence of fifine vertical syndesmophytes associated with concomitant, bilateral sacroiliitis represents the characteristic radiological signs in AS.

    The specifific location of changes in the AS is at the level of:

    ­ the synovial part of the sacroiliac joints (lower half),

    ­ the anterior edges of the vertebral bodies;

  • anterior fifibers of the fifibrous ring ± anterior longitudinal ligament, more fre­ quently affecting the thoracolumbar region.

Spondylolysis begins at the lumbosacral or thoracolumbar junction, subsequently having a progressive character. In the peripheral region, the large proximal joints are affected: hip, shoulder and knee. Affected entheses are located axially and proximal. Diffuse osteopenia is also detected radiologically.

14.3. Metabolic joint disease

14.3.1. Gout

Gout is a metabolic disorder characterized by monosodium urate monohydrate crystals in the synovial flfluid and leukocytes, which causes recurrent episodes of arthritis. In many cases, coarse sodium urate deposits, called tophi are found in the periarticular soft tissues. Gout can be primary or secondary. The primary variant is due to altered purine metabolism or idiopathic reduction of renal urate excretion. At the same time, secondary gout is due to increased serum uric acid (neoplasms, lymphoproliferative diseases, drug treatment: diuretics, ethanol, cytotoxic). The onset age is decades 3-6, male being more affected

Fig. 104. Gout: note interphalangeal osteolysis (M: F = 20: 1). There is also an increased family incidence (6-80%).

Clinic. Patients diagnosed with gout have sudden pain in the 1st MTF joint, usually on the right side. Gout tophi appear after 10-12 years of disease and may have atypical clinical signs: swelling and erythema, without joint or erosive changes; with pseudotumor or infectious appearance. In rare cases, they can cause nerve compression.

Relevant pathology. Deposits of sodium urate appear at the level of the cartilages, epiphyses, periarticular bones and kidneys. Tophi appear as amorphous crystals or masses of urates, which produce a perilesional inflflammatory reaction. In the synovial flfluid, there are crystals with negative birefringence, but also leukocytes in large quantities.

Imaging aspects. Dense tophi and erosions have a characteristic appearance: juxta­articular with prominent edges, perpendicular to the underlying bone, with of the toe (arrow).

14. IINFLAMMATIO dimensions from a few mm to a few cm, are revealed on radiological examinations. Most often, the changes are located at the 1st MTF joint.

RX appearance may be normal in the fifirst 7-10 years of illness. Bone density is, classically, normal. Cartilage destruction occurs late. Erosions are well defifined, with sclerotic rims (prominent, usually intra­articular, but can also be juxta­articular). Tophi appear as nodules with amorphous density, sometimes with distinct calcififications. The location is eccentric, most of the time, not necessarily associated with the joint. Sometimes they can be found as intraosseous calcififications, less often producing a pseudotumor aspect due to large tophi, which cause signifificant bone destruction (fifigure 104).

CT shows the same changes as RX.

MRI identififies intraarticular collection, synovial hypertrophy, postcontrast uptake, bone edema and adjacent soft­tissue edema and erosions with intra­ or juxta-articular localization. In T1-weighted sequences, tophi show a homogeneous intermediate signal. In the T2-weighted and ONS OF THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM l 127 flfluid-sensitive sequences, a mixed, inhomogeneous signal appears, variable depending on the calcium content and the intra­ or extraosseous location.

Ultrasonography accurately establishes the diagnosis of intra-articular flfluid collections. Deposits of urate crystals (hyperechoic), erosions and tophi (nodules with variable echogenicities, depending on density) are visualized on US.

Examination algorithm. The diagnosis is usually made by X­ray examination. US or MRI highlights the tophi in the soft tissues.

THM: Gout is a common condition, which can present any aspect, with any location! The diagnosis is usually made by X­ray examination. The interpretation of the MRI aspect in such cases must be performed in conjunction with the X­ray. The aspirate analysis obtained under imaging guidance may be helpful in the case of differential diagnostic problems. Suggested reading – see chapter 11

Osteoarthritis (Arthrosis)

Carolina Solomon, Man

15.1. General characteristics of osteoarthritis – clinical presen- tation, pathology, imaging

Clinic. Patients have activity­related pain that is reduced at rest. Self­limiting morning stiffness associated with crackling and reduced mobility is common. There are no Celsian signs. Signifificant discrepancies between the patients’ symptoms, primarily pain, and imaging changes are common.

Relevant pathology. Cracks appear at the cartilage level, followed by depressions and ulcerations associated with the reaction of the adjacent bone. Synovial appearance is normal or with minimal inflflammatory changes.

Imaging. Degenerative changes have four primary characteristics:

  • - articular cartilage thickness reduction, which causes narrowing of the joint space, without the appearance of ankylosis;
  • - subchondral sclerosis caused by the repair processes and remodeling;
  • - osteophytosis with peripheral, marginal location, determined by the repair processes at the site of areas not subjected to stress;
  • - cysts or pseudocysts caused by microfractures and the intrusion of synovial flfluid into the altered cancellous bone, following bone contusions.< nuela Lenghel

    15.2. Osteoarthritis of the spine

    Osteoarthritis of the spine is a non­inflflammatory arthropathy, in which cartilage loss occurs, associated with hypertrophic bone changes. Several terms are used to locate arthritic changes in the spine:

  • - osteoarthritis or arthrosis, in the case of synovial joints (atlanto­axial, interapo­ physeal, costovertebral and sacroiliac);
  • - degenerative disc disease, in case of lesions localized at the level of intervertebral disks;
  • - spondylolysis (deformans), related to the vertebral bodies and the fifibrous ring;
  • - diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, in the case of fifibrous joints, ligaments or entheses.

All of these locations may coexist in the same patient. These degenerative changes usually occur in people over the age of 65 and affect about 80% of the population over 75. Women are affected more often than men.

Imaging. The distinctive aspects consist of bone productions at the vertebral bodies, articular facets and uncovertebral joints, generally associated with degenerative disc changes. Depending on the location, several terms are used:

  • - spondylosis, in which the anterior and lateral face of the vertebral bodies are affected;< ­ arthrosis of the small, posterior joint when it involves the articular facets;
  • - for localization at the level of uncovertebral joints, the term uncarthrosis is used.

Osteophytes have variable sizes, ranging from delicate, linear in appearance to large, coarse dimensions. From a morphological point of view, bone formation with typical structure appears. In the case of large osteophytes, the hypertrophic bone contains bone marrow. Osteophytes must be differentiated from syndesmophytes (see Table IX).

X-ray shows normal bone density, associated with subchondral sclerosis of the vertebral plateaus. Spondylosis is characterized by osteophytes’ appearance at the edge of the vertebral plateaus, next to the disc, which is usually narrowed (fifigure 105).

The changes at the cervical posterolateral joints’ level, with bone productions visible in the three planes, are reunited under the term uncarthrosis. The increase in facet density and the appearance of bone productions in the foraminal space characterize the osteoarthritis of the articular facets. Osteophytes are identifified around the odontoid and the anterior arch of the atlas and the ossifification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. The presence of coarse osteophytes around the spinous processes is called Baastrup’s disease. At the sacroiliac joints level, sclerosis is found along the cortex of the synovial region and marginal osteophytes.

On CT, the described bone productions are displayed. Additional fifindings are herniated discs, spinal or foraminal stenosis and hypertrophy of the yellow ligaments (fifigure 106).

Disc herniation and annular lesions are best seen on MRI. Hypertrophy of the ligamentum flflavum, visualized in hyposignal, may cause spinal stenosis. The synovial cysts at the facets’ level can lead to compression or stenosis, respectively narrowing the foraminal space.

Complications occur as a result of the progression of degenerative changes.

Degenerative spondylolisthesis is one of the most common complications. It occurs due to degenerative changes in the intervertebral discs and apophyseal joints and consists of the anterior displacement (sliding) of one vertebra on top of the lower one. This aspect is easily visualized on profifile radiographs. The preferred location is at

Imaging shows narrowing of the joint space, marginal osteosclerosis, osteophytes, and the upper vertebra sliding from the lower one (fifigure 107).

In many cases, the “vacuum phenomenon” aspect is identifified, which consists of a transparent line on the X­ray examination along the intervertebral disc and is produced by the presence of gas inside the disc.

Spinal stenosis will be treated in the Neurology chapter, together with the herniated disc.

15.3. Osteoarthritis of the hip joint (Coxarthrosis)

Coxarthrosis is a non-inflflammatory arthropathy, with loss of cartilage and hypertrophic bone changes. It usually occurs in people over 65, affecting about 80% of the population over 75. The condition is more common in male than in female patients.

Imaging: the degenerative changes are located mainly at the weight support portion (anterosuperior) of the joint.

RX shows normal bone density and focal narrowing of the joint space in the weight support portion. Osteophytes appear in a ring along with the femoral head, larger inferno­medially and at the acetabu­

Fig. 108. Coxarthrosis: the osteophytes induce a note the marked narrowing of the joint space and sl present at the inferior margin of the right hip joint, as

15. OSTEOARTHRITIS (ARTHROSIS) l 131 lar margin. Subchondral cysts have a more prominent acetabular appearance but may be isolated or mimic tumors. Subluxation of the femoral head, especially superomedial, leading to acetabular protrusion may also be encountered. Specifific morphological changes can cause secondary osteoarthritis: femoral­acetabular impingement syndrome, Legg­Calve­Perthes disease, developmental hip dysplasia (DDS), Paget’s disease, inflflammatory arthritis or fractures of the femoral head (fifigure 108).

MRI identififies bone edema, nonspecifific but correlated with pain intensity, X­ray changes, and the number of microfractures in the subchondral bone. Cartilage defects are also better visualized, especially in intraarticular effusion, labral lesions and subchondral or paralabral cysts. Contrast examinations (arthro CT / MRI) allow better visualization of cartilage changes.

Examination algorithm. The best method for diagnosing intermediate forms is an X­ray. MRI is indicated for incipient changes in cartilage or labrum. an opaque rim around the left hip joint (arrowheads); light deformity of the femoral head; osteophytes are s well (arrow). 132 l II. THM: in addition to the general changes, in the case of hip osteoarthritis, the protrusion of the femoral head must be evaluated, and if the changes occur in young adults, investigating the secondary etiology is required.

15.4 Osteoarthritis of the knee joint (Gonarthrosis)

Gonarthrosis is a non-inflflammatory arthropathy, with loss of cartilage and hypertrophic bone changes. 25% of adults over 55 years of age have pain in the knee joint, half of them showing X­rays signs of osteoarthritis, the rest may have signs only on MRI. The Framingham study showed the presence of symptomatic gonarthrosis in 6.1% of adults aged over 30.

Imaging. The best indicator for the diagnosis of gonarthrosis is the visualization on X-ray of the narrowing of the joint space associated with the presence of osteophytes. The articular space appears modifified at the level of both the femoro­tibial joint and the femoro­patellar one. MRI allows the highlighting of the focal or diffuse cartilage defect associated with osteophytes.

There is a narrowing of the joint space, evaluated on X­ray in the AP view.

The most common location of osteo- phytes is at the tibial level (marginal, tibial ridge). Subchondral localization of osteophytosis is rare but with more severe symptoms and cartilaginous lesions (fifigure 109).

Subchondral cysts are also observed.

The articular alignment appears modifified, in varus or valgus, sometimes with patellar subluxation, frequently lateral. Bone density may be normal, with the presence of subchondral sclerosis. Enthesopathy at the quadriceps tendon level (on the upper edge of the patella) is a sign identifified in the axial incidence. Performing the weight­bearing X­ray reveals the varus deformity of the knee.

CT is mainly used to quantify patellar or trochlear dysplasia and “patellar tracking” changes (sliding of the patella relative to the femur during flflexion-extension movements).

MRI visualizes osteophytosis in T1-weighted sequences. Fluid-sensitive sequences, especially PDFS and T2 FS, are used to assess cartilage damage. Bone edema is T2 hyperintense, being correlated, in many cases, with the pain felt by patients. Lesions or degenerations in the menisci are best highlighted in PD sequences. In the advanced stages of the disease, a meniscal protrusion is frequently encountered, correlated with the narrowing of the articular space visible at the X­ray examination. Thickening of the synovial fold is associated with cartilaginous lesions. Collateral or cruciate ligament injuries can also be seen.

Baker cysts (synovial cysts located in the posterior compartment of the knee joint, typically on the medial slope, at the level of the recess between the medial gastrocnemius and semimembranous muscle, communicating with the joint space) are very well highlighted by US (fifigure 110).

Examination algorithm. X­ray examination is the best imaging method used to diagnose osteoarthritis in the moderate or advanced stages. The incipient degradation of cartilage before the appearance of osteophytes is best visualized by MRI.

THM: MRI detects incipient cartilaginous lesions. In the case of meniscal lesions, adjacent cartilaginous lesions should be sought. Bone edema without traumatic cause may indicate the existence of a cartilaginous lesion. Identifification of osteophytes is mandatory for the diagnosis of osteoarthritis.

15.5. Osteoarthritis of the hands

Osteoarthritis of the hands is usually found in people over 65, affecting 80% of the population over 75. The condition is more common in women than in men, the erosive form having an even greater predilection for women (M: F = 1:12).

Imaging. The specifific localization of the typical primary osteoarthritis is at the level of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints; fifirst carpometacarpal (CMC) joint and scaphoid­trapeze­trapezoid (STT) joint. Post­traumatic secondary arthrosis involves the following joints: ulno­lunate, ulno­pyramidal, and scaphoid­radial. From a morphological point of view, the typical osteoarthritis is of pure, productive type, with osteophytes.

At X-ray, the bone density appears within normal limits, mentioning that there may be age­related osteoporosis. The joint hanges. space is usually narrowed symmetrically. Osteoporosis is usually located in the dorsal IP space, being better visualized in the lateral incidence. Osteophytes located at the 1st CMC joint can be very large, especially on the radial side. The modifification of the bone alignment represents another essential aspect in evaluating osteoarthritis, with frequent radial subluxation of MC 1 in the CMC 1 joint.

In the erosive form, the IP joints look like a “seagull’s wing”. This appearance can also occur at the CMC 1 or STT level. Subchondral cysts are also detected on X­Ray. The changes are generally symmetrical, but the disease’s progression may be faster in the dominant hand (fifigure 111).

CT and MRI examinations are not used for the diagnosis of osteoarthritis.

US highlights intra­articular collection, synovial inflflammation, changes in joint space and osteophytes.

Examination algorithm. The diagnosis is established by using X­ray examinations.

16.1. Basics of musculoskeletal tumors imaging

16.1.1. Lesion detection and the risk of sarcomas

Primary bone tumors are relatively uncommon, malignant tumors being by far less frequent than the benign ones. The actual incidence of benign primary bone tumors is unknown, as these are asymptomatic and often detected incidentally. For example, the incidence of bone sarcoma is estimated at 0.8/100,000 individuals (rare before fifive years of age). While some tumors or pseudotumoral bone lesions are easily diagnosed by X­ray examination, many require additional imaging investigations. The diagnosis and staging of osteoarticular tumors represent a challenge and depend on their appearance.

When assessing bone tumors, it is important to take into consideration the relative incidence of the lesions. Enchondroma and non-ossifying fifibroma/benign fifibrous cortical defect are the most frequent benign bone lesions, while bone metastases (> 45 years of age) and multiple myeloma are the most frequent malignant lesions. There are also various disorders associated with the development of bone tumors, which are demonstrated by clinical examination or by imaging. la Lenghel, Csaba Csutak

A high risk of sarcomas is indicated by specifific preexisting lesions, such as enchondroma (especially Ollier and Maffucci disease, which may degenerate into chondrosarcoma) or familial retinoblastoma syndrome (for osteosarcoma).

The following conditions present a moderate risk: osteochondroma for chondrosarcoma; Paget disease and previous irradiation for osteosarcoma or other sarcomas.

Low risk of association with malignant pathology is related to bone infarction, fifibrous dysplasia, chronic osteomyelitis, metal and polyethylene implants, osteoblastoma, giant cell tumor and chondroblastoma.

One of the essential elements for diagnosing tumors of the osteoarticular system is the differentiation between their benign and malignant nature.

    16.2. Tumors of bone origin

    16.2.1. Benign – Osteoma

    Osteoma is a benign tumor consisting of well­differentiated mature bone. The incidence is 3% of the general population, with a higher frequency in male patients (M: F=2:1).

    Clinical picture: Usually, they are asymptomatic, being detected incidentally. In some cases, the tumor affects the sinus drainage with mucocele formation.

    Pathology: Osteoma is a well­differentiated tumor formed by compact bone, without signs of aggressiveness. It is generally a single tumor located subperiosteally in the skull, paranasal sinuses or orbital flfloor: 75% of the cases are located in the paranasal sinuses (frontal > ethmoid > maxillary > sphenoid). Multiple osteomas appear in Gardner’s syndrome.

    Imaging aspects: The mean size is 1-4 cm. The shape is round or oval, with smooth, sessile or pedunculated margins in the case of sinus location.

    X-ray or CT - Osteoma appears as an opaque, round-oval mass attached to the bone cortex; it may become multilobulated during evolution, with a regular outline, precise delineation, homogeneous structure, without periosteal reaction and soft tissue masses (fifigure 113).

    Examination algorithm: The diagnosis is established by X­ray. CT examination allows a better characterization of the lesions, especially in large size lesions, with inhomogeneous appearance.

    Important: Osteoma is located mainly in the paranasal sinuses, having an opaque

    16.2.2. Malignant – Osteosarcoma

    Osteosarcoma is one of the most frequent non­hematological malignant primary bone tumors (20%). Osteosarcoma produces an osteoid matrix with various histological types. Most osteosarcomas do not have a known cause, being considered idiopathic. Secondary causes of osteosarcoma are Paget’s disease and post­radiotherapy. Osteosarcoma is more frequent in men (M:F=3:1).

    Clinical picture: Signs and symptoms are usually non-specifific: deep, resistant, non-specifific pain, associated with adjacent soft tissue edematous changes, palpable mass and functional limitation. In many cases, the fifirst presentation to the doctor can be due to a pathological bone fracture.

    Relevant morphopathology: There are several histological types depending on bone location:

  • intramedullary (80%);< -cortical or juxtacortical (10-15%): paros teal osteosarcoma, periosteal osteosar­ coma; 5 % - other locations.

Regarding skeletal location, osteosarcomas most frequently develop in the long bone metaphysis (70-80%): femur, tibia and humerus, according to the so­called sarcoma location rule “close to the knee, away from the elbow”.

Imaging aspects:

X-ray shows destructive, infifiltrative, eccentric lesions in the metaphysis or diaphysis (epiphyseal extension in 75%), with a large transition area, without osteosclerotic margins or with the loss of the trabecular structure. Density varies between osteolytic lesions and an intensely sclerotic appearance, and the presence of the matrix is visible in most cases. Bone destruction with soft tissue tumor mass is evidenced. PeriORS OF THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM l 139 osteal reaction is aggressive, having a spic- ulated sunburst or interrupted appearance: Codman triangle (fifigure 114, also see fifigure 112). CT is rarely necessary; it has a role in guiding bone biopsy and staging distant metastases. The tumor is highly vascular with early metastases to the lung.

MRI is extremely useful in local staging, in assessing tumor extension to soft tissues and identifying potential skip lesions.

Examination algorithm: Diagnosis is generally established by X­ray. MRI is the method of choice for local tumor staging and restaging after chemotherapy.

Highly malignant tumor with bone origins (medullary region).

16.3. Tumors of cartilaginous origin

16.3.1. Benign 16.3.1.1. Chondroma

Chondroma (enchondroma – centrally located) is a benign intramedullary tumor mass with a cartilage matrix. It develops during childhood or young adulthood and is usually detected incidentally (the second most common chondroid lesion). Regarding location, most chondromas occur in the medullary cavity of tubular bones. The typical location is in the hands and feet

17. TUMO (50%). It is found only in bones formed by enchondral ossifification (never in the skull).

Clinical picture: It is usually asymptomatic, being detected incidentally. Pathological fractures occur frequently.

Relevant pathology: The cartilage matrix represents the morphological substrate. The presence of multiple enchondromas occurs in Ollier disease, which affects the appendicular skeleton, and sarcomatous transformation may appear in 25-30% of cases. Maffucci’s syndrome is characterized by multiple enchondromas and phleboliths (unilateral in 50%).

Imaging aspects:

X-ray typically reveals lytic lesions 1-2 cm in size, located in the medullary bone. Most of them are in the metaphysis and diaphysis, rarely in the epiphysis. They have multilobulated margins, sometimes extending to the cortical bone. There are ring- and arc-like chondroid calcififications without periosteal reaction (fifigure 116).

MRI demonstrates multilobulated intramedullary masses in T1 isosignal or hyposignal, predominantly T2 hypersignal (hyaline cartilage ­ water).

16.3.1.2. Osteochondroma

This lesion represents 10-15% of all bone tumors, 20-50% of benign tumors. Synonym: exostosis. It develops during childhood and is usually detected incidentally. Osteochondromas may be solitary or multiple – multiple hereditary exostoses. Very rarely, they may undergo malignant transformation. The location is mainly in the lower limbs (50%), most of them in the distal third of the femur. They stop growing with skeletal maturity.

Clinical picture: Osteochondromas are benign masses with slow growth, usually asymptomatic, detected incidentally. Symptoms may occur following local injuries (mass effect on nerves or blood vessels, local soft tissue inflflammation). 142 l II. THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM

16.4. Round cell tumors

16.4.1. Multiple myeloma

It is the most common primary bone neoplasm in adults, with unknown etiology, associated with some predisposing factors: herbicides, insecticides, benzene or radiation. It occurs in persons aged over 40, being more frequent in men.

It is located in areas containing bloodforming bone marrow, more often in the axial than in the appendicular skeleton, more frequently proximal than distal. The lesions have variable sizes.

Clinical picture: The most frequent sign is bone pain, associated with hematological and urinary changes (Bence­Jones proteinuria).

Imaging aspects:
